text: Straight from Databricks' own framing: agentic data engineering is the shift from manually hand-coding and monitoring pipelines to using autonomous AI agents that understand your enterprise context to author, operate, and troubleshoot your data workflows. This chapter is organized around seven genuinely new capabilities announced at Data + AI Summit 2026, one per lesson.

That's three distinct verbs. Some of the next seven lessons are about authoring faster — Lakeflow Designer and Genie Code. Some are about operating with less manual toil — Genie ZeroOps. And one, Zerobus Ingest, is about an entirely new way to get data into the lakehouse in the first place, no message bus required.

Here's the problem a general-purpose coding assistant runs into that a data-engineering-specific agent doesn't: an agent can write flawless Python and still fail if it doesn't know which upstream definition of revenue to use. A generic coding agent has no access to your lineage graph and no visibility into the governance policies that should constrain what it's allowed to touch.

Lakeflow — the umbrella you've already met across Chapters 2 through 4 — now spans three areas. Unified data engineering is what this course already taught you: connecting, transforming, and orchestrating under one governed platform. Agentic development and autonomous operations are what's genuinely new, and they only became possible because that first row already existed.

Four concrete pressures motivate everything in the rest of this chapter: tool sprawl blocking AI work before it starts, a maintenance burden where teams spend over half their time fighting silent failures, blind cron-based orchestration guessing at data readiness, and dual-engine complexity forcing teams to bolt on a second engine just for real-time latency. Each of the next seven lessons answers one of these directly.
Next lesson: Zerobus Ingest — the API that lets a producing application push event data directly into a Delta table, eliminating the message-bus hop entirely.
